Cyprus Faces Economic Strain as UK Tariffs Disrupt Key Exports

Cyprus is grappling with significant economic disruption after the United Kingdom imposed broad-based tariffs on a range of Cypriot goods, raising concerns across the island’s export-driven economy. The new tariffs, implemented abruptly last week, affect sectors from building materials and agriculture to manufactured products. 

The British government cited “market integrity and security concerns” in announcing the move, which has already sent shockwaves through Cyprus’s business community. The UK is one of Cyprus’s most important non-EU trading partners, accounting for an estimated €300 million in annual exports.

Among the companies hit is Vassiliko Cement Works Ltd, a major player in the country’s construction supply chain. “This is a serious blow,” said Andreas Christou, spokesperson for Vassiliko Cement Works Ltd. “We export significant volumes to the UK market. The new tariffs make our products less competitive overnight and force us to reevaluate our production pipeline.”

Other firms across the food and beverage, chemicals, and light manufacturing sectors are reporting shipment delays and contract renegotiations as British importers pause or reduce orders. The Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates that exports affected by the tariffs represent nearly 10% of the nation’s total goods trade.

“Cyprus’s export sector is highly diversified, so the impact is being felt widely,” said Eleni Papadopoulou, a trade analyst at the Cypriot Economic Institute. “While some industries may be able to shift to alternative markets, the UK remains a critical destination for many small and mid-sized exporters.”

The Cyprus Ministry of Energy, Commerce and Industry has called for urgent talks with British counterparts. “We are actively engaging to resolve this situation, which threatens jobs and businesses across Cyprus,” said Minister Giorgos Papageorgiou in a statement.

Trade unions have also voiced concern about potential job losses, warning the situation could worsen if the tariffs remain in place. With no resolution yet in sight, Cypriot authorities and businesses are bracing for continued uncertainty and economic fallout in the coming weeks.
